Title: Melatonin Receptor 1 Deficiency Affects Feeding Dynamics and Pro-Opiomelanocortin Expression in the Arcuate Nucleus and Pituitary of Mice.

Journal/Date: Neuroendocrinology (2017)

MeSH Keywords: Animals, Arcuate Nucleus of Hypothalamus, Circadian Rhythm, Eating, Feeding Behavior, Gene Expression Regulation, Locomotion, Male


--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND/METHODS]: Melatonin, the neurohormone for darkness, mediates photoperiod-dependent changes in physiology and behavior by targeting specific membrane-bound receptors (MT1 and MT2). In the present study, we investigated the impact of MT1 receptor deficiency on feeding behavior, locomotor activity and mRNA expression levels encoding for the polypeptide pro-opiomelanocortin (Pomc) and neuropeptide Y (Npy) in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) and the adenohypophysis [pars distalis (PD) and pars intermedia (PI)] in a comparison between wild-type (WT) and MT1-deficient (MT1-/-) mice.
[RESULTS]: The MT1-/- mice spent significantly more time feeding than the WT mice, while the general locomotor behavior, body weight and the total amount of food consumed did not differ between both genotypes. The nocturnal expression levels of Pomc in the ARC and PD were significantly higher in WT as compared to MT1-/- mice and exogenous melatonin administered during the light phase stimulated Pomc expression in WT mice only. No differences were found between WT and MT1-/- mice with regard to Pomc expression levels in the PI.
[CONCLUSION]: Thus, the MT1-mediated signaling stimulates Pomc expression in a region-specific pattern. Since the MT1-mediated changes in Pomc expression do not elicit direct orexigenic or anorexigenic effects, such effects are obviously mediated by regulatory systems downstream of the Pomc mRNA (e.g. cleavage and release of POMC derivatives), which are independent of MT1 signaling.

key_findings.finding: The directly relevant mouse study is Jilg et al., Neuroendocrinology (2017), PMID 27490331, titled “Melatonin Receptor 1 Deficiency Affects Feeding Dynamics and Pro-Opiomelanocortin Expression in the Arcuate Nucleus and Pituitary of Mice.” It compared male wild-type and MT1/Mel1a-deficient (MT1−/−; corresponding to Mtnr1a loss) mice, assessing feeding behavior, locomotor activity, body weight/food intake, and Pomc/Npy mRNA in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) and pituitary pars distalis (PD) and pars intermedia (PI).

source_tools.relevance: Direct paper abstract and MeSH/design details

key_findings.finding: Receptor-1 deficiency altered feeding dynamics but not gross intake: MT1−/− mice spent significantly more time feeding than WT mice, whereas total food consumed, body weight, and general locomotor behavior did not differ. Thus, the evidence supports a change in feeding pattern/duration, not increased overall caloric intake.

MT1/Mel1a deficiency reduced nocturnal Pomc expression in the arcuate nucleus and pituitary pars distalis: nocturnal Pomc mRNA was significantly higher in WT than MT1−/− mice. Melatonin given during the light phase increased Pomc expression in WT but not MT1−/− mice, supporting an MT1-dependent stimulatory effect. No genotype difference was detected in Pomc expression in the pituitary pars intermedia.

source_tools.relevance: PubTator annotation independently links Mt1/melatonin positively with Pomc

key_findings.finding: Overall yes/no conclusion: Yes—MT1/Mel1a receptor deficiency alters feeding dynamics and decreases nocturnal Pomc expression in the ARC and pars distalis. No—it does not increase total food consumption, and it does not alter Pomc expression in the pars intermedia. The authors further concluded that the Pomc mRNA change did not produce a straightforward orexigenic/anorexigenic phenotype, implying downstream POMC processing/release or other regulatory systems may decouple expression from total intake.
